items.title: ‘Chilling’: As Nepal Grapples With Flooding Chaos, Christians Face Another Potential Horror
items.author: Billy Hallowell
items.summary: Pray.
items.content:
📖 News | Faithwire

As Nepal deals with the horrific toll of tragic flooding that killed more than 1,000 people, at least 20 churches have reportedly been destroyed by the damaging waters.

Joel Veldkamp, head of international communications at Christian Solidarity International (CSI), told CBN News that one congregation has 80 individuals and families who lost their homes — and that’s just one example.

Listen to the latest episode of “Quick Start”

CSI has been working to get food, mattresses, mosquito nets, cleaning supplies, and other items to people in Nepal to help meet basic needs.

Veldkamp said there’s another dynamic unfolding inside the South Asian nation: persecution, an issue gaining steam and attention before the deadly flooding began.

“We’ve seen in the last 10 years … persecution of Christians has spiked in Nepal,” he said. “It wasn’t really a big problem before, and today it’s still not on the scale like we’ll see in India, or Pakistan, or other nearby countries. But there is now a law against conversion, so it’s illegal to try to get someone else to change their religion.”

Veldkamp said this is a violation of human rights standards, but that this law is used to prosecute pastors and missionaries — even Christians who might happen to visit and speak with Hindu friends.

“We have seen an uptick in these cases of Christians being jailed on accusations,” he said, noting that sharing the Gospel can be enough to spark legal chaos.

Veldkamp said there’s a new government in Nepal after the previous regime was overthrown in a revolution. An election unfolded in March, which has only added to the uncertainty.

“We still don’t know really what that means, but the country is in flux [and] is headed in a new political direction,” he said. “There are some good signs and some bad signs from the new government, so Christians in Nepal are very concerned about which way the country is going to go now.”

Nepal is one of two Hindu-majority nations in the world, with India joining it in that distinction. Until 2008, Nepal was a Hindu nation before becoming a federal republic. Today, there are new calls to return to that previous designation — something that should be of concern to Christians and other religious minorities.

India has been reportedly putting pressure on Nepal to embrace Hindu nationalism, funding groups that seek to push Christians to reconvert, among other issues.

“There are serious efforts to change Nepal’s constitution to make it officially a Hindu country again,” Veldkamp said. “And in the current environment, that would mean probably the harassment of Christians. Attacks on churches would only increase because then it would be official that this country does not belong to Christians.”

With pastors, missionaries, and Christians already under fire, he said there’s a “real threat that is having a chilling effect” on believers in Nepal.

“Right now, when these things happen to Christians, Christians can say, ‘Hey, we’re a secular country. Nepal is a country for everyone. It says so in our Constitution,'” Veldkamp said. “And that’s … a good argument. That’s a good lever that they can use to appeal to their fellow Nepali citizens for justice.”

But if Nepal becomes a Hindu nation, these arguments dissipate both legally and in the public sphere. Veldkamp encouraged believers worldwide to pray for the church.

items.title: Pro-Life Group Reportedly Kicked Out of Coffee Shop, Compared to KKK
items.author: Billy Hallowell
items.summary: The founder of a well-known pro-life organization has gone viral in recent days after reportedly being kicked out of an […]
items.content:
📖 News | Faithwire

The founder of a well-known pro-life organization has gone viral in recent days after reportedly being kicked out of an Idaho coffee shop after the owner learned she was holding a meeting there.

Listen to the latest episode of “Quick Start”

Kristan Hawkins, president of Students for Life of America, shared a video of what purportedly took place at Wydaho Roasters last month — and that video went viral.

Hawkins told CBN News that coffee shop owner Jim Sheehan made his displeasure known after she, her son, and others met to discuss pro-life issues inside Wydaho Roasters. Her son’s goal has been to rally people against Proposition 1, an abortion measure that will be on the ballot in November.

“We’re recruiting door knockers, and we’ve had students going door to door, educating people in Idaho about this extreme abortion ballot referendum, which sadly many people don’t know about,” Hawkins said, noting her son rallied people online to come meet to form a pro-life group to address the issue.

The coffee shop was the intended gathering place for the group’s first meeting, but that didn’t go very well.

“We had purchased our drinks and our food,” she said. “Some other leaders, community members, came to kind of join the group that I knew from church.”

According to Hawkins, Sheehan came out of his office and told the group they couldn’t meet at the shop and needed to leave. Hawkins took out her camera and started filming the interaction, hoping she could simply convince the owner to let them stay for the first meeting and then pledge not to return.

“I was trying to negotiate with him, just like, let us finish this meeting; we won’t come back,” she said. “And then he just kept going and then compared us to the KKK and said, we were like the KKK, that pro-lifers were like the KKK, which was just beyond the pale. And that’s actually why I decided to release the video.”

Hawkins made it clear that she believes, as an owner, Sheehan has the right to refuse service and was within his rights to ask the group to leave. That said, she also believes in her right to expose his purported comparison between the pro-life activists and the KKK.

The result of the entire escapade was intense media coverage and viral video discussion. Ultimately, both Hawkins and Sheehan reportedly started getting death threats.

“He was well within his rights to kick us out,” Hawkins said. “I was within my rights to expose his insanity, believing that community members were like the KKK, but neither of us deserves to die or receive death threats.”

Sheehan told Fox News that he pushes back on claims the group was kicked out. He said he had asked via Facebook the day before that the group not meet in his coffee shop.

“Sunday she announced on a local community page they were holding this meeting at our business, naming it — I responded to the post politely asking them not to use our business as the agenda of the organization does not align with us,” he told the outlet. “They showed up anyway.”

items.title: SEU Worship Has a Question About Worship Music: Where Did the Joy Go?
items.author: Emily Brown
items.summary: Chelsea Plank didn’t want “The Cost Is a Joy” on this album. The song came out of a writing session with Cam Giddens and Austin Shuffit, who produces for the group, and when the session ended, what Plank had was an acoustic demo. For her, that’s close to useless. “I nee
items.content:
📖 Culture | Relevant Magazine

Chelsea Plank didn’t want “The Cost Is a Joy” on this album.

The song came out of a writing session with Cam Giddens and Austin Shuffit, who produces for the group, and when the session ended, what Plank had was an acoustic demo. For her, that’s close to useless.

“I need a fully produced-out track at the end of a writing session,” she said. “I don’t have much vision up here when it comes to, like, man, this acoustic track — I’m just not sure how it lands.”

So when the group sat down early in the year to sort through what might make the record, Plank didn’t put it forward. Other people did.

“They were like, let’s just try this out,” she said. “And it has actually been the anthem of my heart now.”

It’s also the song with her name on it. “The Cost Is a Joy” is credited to SEU Worship and Chelsea Plank, and it hands Found in the Field — the group’s new live album, out now — both its argument and its title.

The argument started with something Shuffit had been noticing in Southeastern University’s students. He came up through the school himself before joining staff, and he prefaced the thought carefully.

“This is no shade towards anyone,” he said, at which point Plank cut in: “Gosh, I don’t know what he’s about to say.”

“There is a lot of language around the cost of following Jesus,” he continued. “The suffering of it, the hardship of it. And we just thought it was a fresh and important perspective for our students to have — that yes, there is suffering, but there is joy in this.”

Plank grew up on that language too, and she doesn’t think it’s wrong.

“It is such a powerful message,” she said. “Even when you hear David talking about, I’m not going to give the Lord an offering that costs me nothing. There is a price to following Jesus. It’s your whole life.”

The problem is what happens when the price is all anyone sings about.

“It can turn really legalistic really quick,” she said.

Her alternative puts the events in a different order. The surrender doesn’t come first and the joy doesn’t arrive later as a reward for it — the seeing comes first, and the giving-up follows from it almost as a reflex. “Out of the abundance of our heart of seeing him, of needing to know him — that’s easy. I will give up everything, and the cost is a joy.”

She has a line for this: “The kingdom of heaven is made up of righteousness, peace and joy. Joy is a third of the kingdom. Joy is the serious business of heaven, we like to say.”

The album title comes from the same place — the parable in Matthew where the kingdom is a treasure buried in a field, and the man who finds it sells everything he owns to buy the land. The transaction only makes sense if you know what’s in the ground. Not, as Plank puts it, “a begrudging act of surrender, but a joyful act of servitude.”

There’s a second reading of the phrase she likes as much: being found in the field of God’s presence, and staying there. “Giving up everything to remain there.”

Made for One Room

None of these songs arrived as an album. They arrived as chapel services.

SEU Worship is the worship movement at Southeastern University, an Assemblies of God school in Lakeland, Florida, and the group’s records are assembled backward from what already works in the room. Songs get played on campus for months before anyone decides whether they’re worth recording.

“When you hear an album of ours, usually we’ve been playing it all year on our campus,” Plank said. “It’s almost like a yearbook of our year. A snapshot of our year.”

“We play them on campus first to see if they even resonate with our community, or if they even work. And then what’s working in chapel and in our community is usually what makes the records every time.”

It’s a filter that runs in the opposite direction from most of the industry, where a song is written to travel and then handed to a congregation. Plank’s advice to other churches making music is to stop reaching so far.

“It is first and foremost for your community,” she said. “Who did God call you to steward? I can’t steward the nation. I can’t disciple the world.”

Even the writing sessions start there: “What’s the language that our community is missing? What concept do you feel like we’re needing to sing about?”

Rooms That Used to Be Empty

That approach got tested this summer, when SEU Worship — coming off a 10-day outpouring on campus in February that drew national attention — took songs written for one chapel out on its first headlining tour. The group also served as its own setup and teardown crew.

“We set up all the stage design, lighting, all the booths that we had,” Plank said, calling it a boots-on-the-ground experiment and, unexpectedly, a bonding one.

What Shuffit remembers is the singing.

“We were filling a room with young adults and people from all age groups and doing like two hours of worship, only playing our songs,” he said. “Me and Chelsea have both been a part of SEU Worship long enough to know that there were times in the early days where that wasn’t always possible. There wasn’t always a room full of people that could sing our songs.”

“That was a very sobering and humbling realization.”

The song he keeps coming back to isn’t the one Plank almost left off. It’s “Bless the Blood,” written in an unusually small room — just him, Plank and Caylie Bryant.

“We had to fight for it,” he said. Months of it, on and off: leaving it, coming back to it, leaving it, coming back to it. It wasn’t finished until the week of the recording.

“The way that it portrays the sacrifice that Christ made for us, and the power that that has, is some of the most moving lyrical content I’ve ever gotten to be a part of.”

As for the song she tried to leave behind, Plank has noticed where it lands hardest, and it isn’t with students. It’s with the people running things.

“Where I’ve seen it connecting specifically is with other church leaders,” she said. “Because of just remembering the why.”

“It’s just a joy to give up our lives for the Gospel.”

items.title: For a More Theological Exploration of the Trojan War, Try ‘Son of Nobody’
items.author: Dr. Alex Taylor
items.summary:
Dr. Alex Taylor

Anyone expecting to open the book so conveniently labeled “a novel” on its cover and find the usual flow of prose will find themselves questioning what’s been put in front of them.
items.content:
📖 Catholic Teaching | Word on Fire

Dr. Alex Taylor

While the Christopher Nolan rendition of the Odyssey was artistically better than expected—and by that I mean narratively and not simply on the level of cinematic techne—one prominent difference from its Homeric source could not be ignored. Nolan’s Odyssey, unlike Homer’s, is one produced by an age of disenchantment, where the gods don’t speak but in the natural language of wave and cloud and thunder, and the apparition that seems a god later appears to be little more than Odysseus’s traumatically damaged memory reasserting itself in the present. Anyone looking for another examination of the war that launched a thousand ships—one more explicitly engaged in theological investigation—should turn to Yann Martel’s new fiction, Son of Nobody.

Martel’s oeuvre, at least since his second novel, the Man-Booker-Prize-winning Life of Pi, has largely been concerned with the problem of evil and therefore with the quest for theodicy, an understanding as to how God can be just while there remains evil in the world. Son of Nobody pirouettes artfully between two main characters, the first being Psoas, Son of Nobody, the Midean nobody whose exploits at Troy the rediscovered poem center upon, and Harlow Donne, the Canadian academic who has pieced that work together from the fragments of Oxyrhinchian papyri. The two men have much in common despite the thousands of years which separate them—they both have left home behind, particularly wives and children, in pursuit of work (for Psoas, war, for Harlow, textual archaeology) commanded by a powerful superior utterly indifferent to their fates despite profound human similarities between their supervisors and themselves. But what they ultimately have in common is suffering and facing down the death of innocents, questioning how the world can continue to turn in the face of such a mystery.

Anyone expecting to open the pages of the book so conveniently labeled “a novel” on its cover and find the usual uninterrupted flow of prose for hundreds of pages at a time will find themselves questioning what exactly it is that’s been put in front of them. Son of Nobody combines a series of poetic fragments in free-verse—although more inspired by Lattimore than Laforgue—with running footnotes, which at times appear scholarly. However, as one reads, Harlow diverges from his role as scholarly commentator and instead inhabiting a narrator role vis-a-vis his own life. The most recent type of such a fiction is of course Nabokov’s Pale Fire (1962), where a lengthy poem by the fictitious poet John Shade is encompassed by editorial materials created by one Charles Kinbote, Shade’s neighbor, academic colleague, and, supposedly, his friend. We come to see, however, that Kinbote has published his edition of Shade without the permission of the latter’s widow and that his notes have less to do with analyzing the poem and more to do with providing a paranoid interpretation of the poem as an esoteric political tale about the last prince of the fictional Eastern European country of Zembla. One of its early critics claimed that “whether it be a novel at all is open to question, so unconventional is its form,” and the same charge can be made of Son of Nobody. But that question—the question of literary form—opens up the fundamental significance of Martel’s fiction, a new episode in the Menippean tradition.

The group of works which came to be grouped together as Menippean satires take their origin from Greek Cynic philosophy, particularly the Cynic philosopher Menippus, whose antics were chronicled by the Hellenistic writer Lucian. Lucian wrote in the second century AD largely satirical works, treating serious things with great humor in the style aptly called spoudaiogeloion, which literally translated means “the serious-comical thing.” While Plato’s dialogues send Socrates into commonplace settings—the Athenian agora, a symposium, or pacing outside the city walls—Lucian’s Dialogues of the Dead send Menippus to Hades, and he’s more often mocking the dead souls for their transgressions than he is engaging in philosophical disputation (although he does that as well). Works of the Menippean tradition have been called an “anti-genre” because while they often have certain features in common—such as the endeavor to combine heterogenous things (prose and poetry, phallic jokes and philosophy), a particular concern with the grotesque, and the equality of mankind before death—they’re an odd bunch of compositions that don’t sit well together. Consider, if you will, Rabelais’s Gargantua and Pantagruel, Cervantes’s Don Quixote, Joyce’s Ulysses—and now, Martel’s Son of Nobody.

Harlow Donne dedicates his translation and editorial work of the fragments of his newly-discovered “Psoad” to his daughter, Helen. His subsequent loss of her draws him into greater sympathy with the characters of Greek epic—in a heated argument with his wife, he implicitly compares himself to Agamemnon, a strange comparison which only makes sense when we understand that Harlow wants to see his suffering as noble and not purposeless or without meaning. 

In Democracy in America, Alexis de Tocqueville suggested that the reading of Greek and Latin literature could be useful to Americans for a similar reason. The classics “marvelously . . . counterbalance our particular defects,” living as we do in a democratic nation. They impart a love of order, a care for detail, “a noble step,” “and the search for ideal beauty constantly shows itself.” The Menippean satire, like the Greek old comedy, tends to deal with low characters rather than high ones; commoners more often are at its heart than kings. But Martel does not show his commoner Psoas as merely ridiculous, but endows him with a peculiar noble dignity in his love for his family which urges him to continue to fight, even a battle which appears unwinnable.

One of the recurrent events within the episodes of the “Psoad” are battlefield encounters between Psoas and Prince Mestor, ostensibly one of Priam’s fifty sons. The first encounter is preceded by a section of the poem “How Men Fought: The Hero and the Ordinary Men,” where, after the poet outlines the advantages of the hero (his god-made armor, his training from youth for battle, and his spiritedness), he nonetheless insists that the roles of the ordinary man and the hero might yet shift in battle, the former fighting with grim resolve, “his face impassive, / his actions quick, his intent precise and deadly, / just as you might see the hero fleeing / like a hare pursued by dogs, face white with fear.” This shift is what we eventually see when Psoas, having grieved for the insult Mestor issues about his wife, finally triumphs, when the prince and commoner fight on shockingly equal terrain, the details of which are not less Greek for being ludicrous in the best sense. 

Less ludicrous is the encounter Psoas has subsequently with Hades himself, who has emerged from the underworld to see the battle which is glutting his kingdom with shades. The presence of Hades provides evidence of Martel’s theological depth. Harlow, annotating this section, seeking consolation for the death of his daughter, constantly thinks about the Greek epic in conversation with “the other foundational book of Western culture, the Gospels.” He sees in the Psoad’s valuation of the common man in his dignity, in his vulnerability to loss, death, and suffering, Psoas’s insistence on and enactment of the truth he proclaims to Mestor—“I am no less of a man than you are”—a precursor to the Gospels. While the metaphysical roots of the claim in the Declaration of Independence that “all men are created equal” can be found in the Book of Genesis that man and woman are created in the image and likeness of God, the incarnation of God in the person of Jesus of Nazareth enacts this truth of human dignity, by revealing his desire to live among mankind and to show us thereby the dignity of the ordinary everyday nature of our existence. Harlow sees the image of Hades desiring to know “the fruit of death” as a revelation that the Incarnation would not be wholly foreign to the Greeks, that even they might have an intuition that the good God might want to be with us in our suffering.

It was Erich Auerbach, in his classic work of literary criticism, Mimesis: The Representation of Reality in Western Literature (1946), who noticed this unique place of the Gospels in Greek literature. Tragedy focused on the serious actions of the serious man; comedy on the unserious actions of the unserious man. But the Gospels, in portraying Peter’s betrayal of Jesus and his agonized contrition, betray the serious action at work in the soul of a low-born fisherman, suggesting that such seriousness is possible for all who come to love the Lord of all mankind. Martel’s work presents this profoundly democratic truth in a literary mode fascinatingly between aristocracy and democracy: a place our nation will need to rediscover for its next two hundred and fifty years.

items.title: Tuesday, September 8, 2026
items.author: Bishop Robert Barron
items.summary:
Bishop Robert Barron

Friends, today we celebrate the Feast of the Nativity of the Blessed Virgin Mary.
items.content:
📖 Catholic Teaching | Word on Fire

Bishop Robert Barron

Daily Reading


First Reading
Micah 5:1-4a

Now you are walled around with a wall;
    siege is laid against us;
with a rod they strike the ruler of Israel
    upon the cheek.
But you, O Bethlehem of Ephrathah,
    who are one of the little clans of Judah,
from you shall come forth for me
    one who is to rule in Israel,
whose origin is from of old,
    from ancient days.
Therefore he shall give them up until the time
    when she who is in labor has brought forth;
then the rest of his kindred shall return
    to the people of Israel.
And he shall stand and feed his flock in the strength of the Lord,
    in the majesty of the name of the Lord his God.
And they shall live secure, for now he shall be great
    to the ends of the earth;

Psalm
Psalm 13:6ab, 6c

I will sing to the Lord,
    because he has dealt bountifully with me.

Gospel Reading
Matthew 1:1-16, 18-23

An account of the genealogy of Jesus the Messiah, the son of David, the son of Abraham.

Abraham was the father of Isaac, and Isaac the father of Jacob, and Jacob the father of Judah and his brothers, and Judah the father of Perez and Zerah by Tamar, and Perez the father of Hezron, and Hezron the father of Aram, and Aram the father of Aminadab, and Aminadab the father of Nahshon, and Nahshon the father of Salmon, and Salmon the father of Boaz by Rahab, and Boaz the father of Obed by Ruth, and Obed the father of Jesse, and Jesse the father of King David.

And David was the father of Solomon by the wife of Uriah, and Solomon the father of Rehoboam, and Rehoboam the father of Abijah, and Abijah the father of Asaph, and Asaph the father of Jehoshaphat, and Jehoshaphat the father of Joram, and Joram the father of Uzziah, and Uzziah the father of Jotham, and Jotham the father of Ahaz, and Ahaz the father of Hezekiah, and Hezekiah the father of Manasseh, and Manasseh the father of Amos, and Amos the father of Josiah, and Josiah the father of Jechoniah and his brothers, at the time of the deportation to Babylon.

And after the deportation to Babylon: Jechoniah was the father of Salathiel, and Salathiel the father of Zerubbabel, and Zerubbabel the father of Abiud, and Abiud the father of Eliakim, and Eliakim the father of Azor, and Azor the father of Zadok, and Zadok the father of Achim, and Achim the father of Eliud, and Eliud the father of Eleazar, and Eleazar the father of Matthan, and Matthan the father of Jacob, and Jacob the father of Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom Jesus was born, who is called the Messiah.

Now the birth of Jesus the Messiah took place in this way. When his mother Mary had been engaged to Joseph, but before they lived together, she was found to be with child from the Holy Spirit. Her husband Joseph, being a righteous man and unwilling to expose her to public disgrace, planned to dismiss her quietly. But just when he had resolved to do this, an angel of the Lord appeared to him in a dream and said, “Joseph, son of David, do not be afraid to take Mary as your wife, for the child conceived in her is from the Holy Spirit. She will bear a son, and you are to name him Jesus, for he will save his people from their sins.” All this took place to fulfill what had been spoken by the Lord through the prophet:

“Look, the virgin shall conceive and bear a son,
    and they shall name him Emmanuel,”

Reflection

Friends, today we celebrate the Feast of the Nativity of the Blessed Virgin Mary. And our Gospel declares that she will be the mother of Jesus, who would be “God with us.”

Mary is a rich and multivalent symbolic figure in all of the Gospels. In Luke’s infancy narrative, she emerges as the spokesperson for ancient Israel, speaking, in her Magnificat, in the words and cadences of Hannah.

In Matthew’s Christmas account, she is compelled to go into exile in Egypt and is then called back to her home, recapitulating thereby the journey of Israel from slavery to freedom. She is thus the symbolic embodiment of faithful and patient Israel, longing for deliverance. 

In John’s Gospel, she is, above all, mother—the physical mother of Jesus and, through him, the mother of all who would come to new life in him. As mother of the Lord, she is, once again, Israel, that entire series of events and system of ideas from which Jesus emerged and in terms of which he alone becomes intelligible.
